name: Database Indexing: B-Trees vs LSM-Trees
tagline: Balancing the RUM Conjecture (Read, Update, Memory amplification) between update-in-place B-Tree pages and append-only LSM-Tree SSTables.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of database storage indexes—from B-Tree page splits and covering indexes to LSM MemTables, Bloom filters, and STCS vs LCS compaction.

spark.summary: B-Trees organize sorted keys into fixed-size mutable pages optimized for fast, predictable point and range reads, whereas LSM-Trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted runs to disk for high write throughput.
spark.keyTakeaway: If disk I/O or compaction stalls threaten tail latency, choose B-Trees for read-heavy OLTP workloads needing predictable p99 read latency and in-place updates; choose LSM-Trees for write-heavy ingestion, time-series, and high-compression workloads.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Storage engines balance three competing costs (**The RUM Conjecture**): **Read Amplification**, **Write (Update) Amplification**, and **Space (Memory) Amplification**.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts B-Tree 3-Level Traversal & Covering Leaf Page (Root Page (RAM) -> Internal [A..M] -> Internal [N..Z] -> Leaf #8812); RocksDB Write-Optimized MemTable, L0/L1 SSTables & Bloom Filters (WAL + MemTable -> L0 SSTables -> L1-Ln Leveled -> Zstd SSTables).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Within LSM-Trees, compaction strategy governs write vs. read vs. space amplification. Monitor `l0_num_files` (approaching `level0_stop_writes_trigger` freezes writes!), pending compaction bytes, and tombstone-to-live-row ratios on LSM nodes; on PostgreSQL B-Trees.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Dive deeper into LSM storage engines, Cassandra tombstone scans, B-Tree type-coercion invalidation, and PostgreSQL VACUUM bloat.

learningJourney.title: What are B-Trees and LSM-Trees

explanation.foundation: Storage engines balance three competing costs (**The RUM Conjecture**): **Read Amplification**, **Write (Update) Amplification**, and **Space (Memory) Amplification**.
explanation.core:
- **B-Trees (Update-in-Place)**: Store sorted keys in fixed-size mutable pages (8 KB in PostgreSQL, 16 KB in InnoDB) with 3–4 levels for 100M+ rows (`O(log N)` reads). Updates modify leaf pages in place via WAL and split full pages.
- **LSM-Trees (Out-of-Place)**: Append writes sequentially to a WAL + in-memory **MemTable** (skiplist), flushing immutable sorted **SSTables** to disk and merging them asynchronously via compaction.

B-Trees organize sorted keys into fixed-size mutable pages optimized for fast, predictable point and range reads, whereas LSM-Trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted runs to disk for high write throughput.

decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.

advanced.finalSummary: Choose B-Trees for read-heavy OLTP workloads needing predictable p99 read latency and in-place updates; choose LSM-Trees for write-heavy ingestion, time-series, and high-compression workloads.
advanced.summary: B-Trees organize sorted keys into fixed-size mutable pages optimized for fast, predictable point and range reads, whereas LSM-Trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted runs to disk for high write throughput.
advanced.keyTakeaway: If disk I/O or compaction stalls threaten tail latency, choose B-Trees for read-heavy OLTP workloads needing predictable p99 read latency and in-place updates; choose LSM-Trees for write-heavy ingestion, time-series, and high-compression workloads.

prerequisites.title: Distributed & Application Caching
prerequisites.summary: Caching keeps a reusable copy of data so an application can avoid repeating a database query, calculation, or network call. It can make responses faster and reduce database load. The trade-off: the copy may be out of date.
